chunks: How motors degrade with age. The question: How do motors perform as they age?
As a motor ages, almost everything gets a little worse, and the symptoms point to the cause. Bearings and grease wear, so friction rises. In a brushed motor the brushes wear down.
Winding insulation slowly breaks down with heat. Magnets can lose strength.
The result is the same motor drawing more current for the same job, running hotter and noisier, and wasting more power.
The best defense is to log measurements and watch the trend.
Think of an old bicycle. The chain dries out, the bearings get gritty, and the brake pads rub. You pedal harder for the same speed, you get warmer, and it squeaks.
Each of those faults leaves its own sign: a gritty hub sounds different from a rusty chain.
The ageing mechanisms all feed back into more current and heat, which accelerates the same mechanisms.
This positive feedback is why degradation tends to accelerate near the end of life and why catching early symptoms pays off.
No-load current: the current needed to spin the motor with no load. It measures friction. Torque constant ( K t ): torque per amp. Weaker magnets lower it.
Bathtub curve: failure rate over life, high at the start, low and flat in the middle, then rising at wear-out. Insulation: the thin coating on the winding wire.
Heat slowly breaks it down.
A 12 volts motor has a 1. 2 ohms winding and makes 0. 02 N·m per amp. It carries a 0. 04 N·m load. New, it needs 0. 15 amps just to beat friction, so it draws 0. 04 over 0.
02 plus 0. 15 equals 2. 15 amps and runs near 4500 rpm at about 73% efficiency. Age it: 10% weaker magnets, friction current up to 0. 4 amps, and 5% more resistance.
It now draws about 2. 6 amps, runs slightly faster, and is only about 61% efficient. Weak magnets do not make a slower motor. They make a hungrier one. That is the whole idea.
"Motors drift as they age. Bearings wear and grease degrades, so friction and no-load current rise, with more noise and heat.
Brushes shorten and the commutator grooves, increasing contact resistance and sparking.
Insulation ages and can short turns; magnets can lose strength, lowering the torque constant so you need more current per newton-metre.
Efficiency falls, a 73 percent motor might drop to 61. Reliability follows a bathtub curve, so I'd trend current, vibration and temperature to catch wear-out early."
